# Novelty check for candidates A–H

| | Candidate | Verdict | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Anchoring process models on the Open Anchoring Quest (OpAQ) | PARTLY DONE | medium-high |
| B | Social-influence revision model tested out of sample across datasets | PARTLY DONE | medium |
| C | Bayesian sampler on forecasting tournaments | NOVEL in application; the core idea is partly anticipated | medium-high |
| D | Many Labs heterogeneity caused by scale, baseline or reliability | PARTLY DONE, with an active competing group | medium-high |
| E | Small-sample model predicting feedback shifts and the description–experience gap | PARTLY DONE | medium |
| F | Hard–easy effect across the Confidence Database | PARTLY DONE | medium |
| G | Advice taking as Bayesian cue integration giving trimodal weights | PARTLY DONE | medium-high |
| H | Inner crowd as an autocorrelated sampler, as a function of delay | NOVEL as specified | medium-high |

H and C are the most open. D has a live competing research group.

I checked A, B and C myself. D–H come from subagent reports that I spot-checked against my own OpenAlex and Crossref searches. All DOIs are as returned by OpenAlex or Crossref.

**Correction to the brief:** the Herzog & Hertwig 2009 DOI given in the task returns a 404. The resolving DOI is https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2009.02271.x.

## A. Anchoring process models on OpAQ
**Papers citing the OpAQ data paper (10.5334/jopd.67):** OpenAlex lists four, and none models OpAQ.
- https://doi.org/10.1177/09567976241252138 (2024): anchors half a crowd low and half high to improve the crowd average.
- https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/wvfm3: preprint of the same paper.
- https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-025-00276-9 (2025): "range nudges", i.e. anchors in behavioural guidelines.
- https://doi.org/10.5334/jopd.92: correction notice for the data paper.

**Closest papers:**
- **Röseler & Schütz 2022**, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn (preprint). Meta-analysis of OpAQ, k = 393.
  - Extremity was measured as |anchor − true value| / true value.
  - The effect was positive (b = .040, p < .001), described as "nonlinear but positive".
  - The inverted U predicted by selective accessibility "was not supported".
  - No process model was fitted. Knowledge was not tested.
- **Schley & Weingarten 2026**, https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03238. Meta-analysis of 2,601 effect sizes.
  - Extremity was coded only as binary (authors called the anchor "extreme"). The effect was null.
  - Knowledge showed a small reduction.
  - The paper lists the inverted-U prediction from the plausibility/attitude-change account (Wegener et al. 2001).
- **Turner & Schley 2016**, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2016.07.003. Anchor Integration Model: Bayesian inverse-variance weighting, fitted to the authors' own experiments. This is the natural quantitative competitor to Lieder's model.
- **Lieder et al. 2018**, https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8 and https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1288-6. Qualitative simulations of ten classic effects, including extremity and uncertainty, plus two new experiments.

**Answers:**
- (a) No process model has been fitted to OpAQ.
- (b) Extremity has been tested as a moderator, but only with coarse, study-level measures. Uncertainty has only been tested as a binary "knowledge" code.
- (c) Inverted U versus monotone has been tested once, coarsely, with a monotone result.

**Still open:** item-level fits of Lieder's model against the Anchor Integration Model and a plausibility model, the concavity prediction with distance in SD units, and continuous item uncertainty.

**Data limit:** OpAQ has no unanchored SD per item, so SD scaling needs a proxy.

## B. Social-influence revision model, cross-dataset out-of-sample test
**Closest papers:**
- **Almaatouq et al. 2022**, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-20551-7 (preprint https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/f5ky3).
  - Pools four datasets with 2,885 participants: Lorenz 2011, Becker 2017, Gürçay 2015 and Becker 2019.
  - Uses a DeGroot-type framework (a weighted-averaging model of opinion updating), showing the effect depends on how centralised influence is and on the spread of initial estimates.
  - Descriptive and theoretical. No fitted revision model is used to predict other datasets.
- **Pilgrim & Becker 2024**, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2407.00199. Splits the change in group error into three terms and checks this against six published experiments:
  - how centralised the influence network is;
  - "calibration" (whether more accurate people are more influential);
  - "herding" (whether people near the average are more influential).
  It is a model-based pooled analysis, but it does not predict error change per question from fixed parameters.
- **Jayles et al. 2017**, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1703695114, and **Kao et al. 2018**, https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2018.0130. Revision models that depend on distance and direction, fitted and validated within each paper's own data.
- **Becker et al. 2017**, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1615978114. Correlation between revision and accuracy; within-study only.

**Still open:** fit a revision model on one dataset, freeze its parameters, and predict the per-question change in crowd error in the other datasets. The pooled analyses above are the benchmarks it must beat.

## C. Bayesian sampler applied to forecasting tournaments
- Citers of Zhu 2020, Sundh 2023 and Costello & Watts 2014 return zero hits for "extremiz" and "aggregat". "Forecast" hits are unrelated (random-walk prediction, poker).

**Closest papers:**
- **Baron et al. 2014**, https://doi.org/10.1287/deca.2014.0293. Gives two reasons to extremize the aggregate:
  1. Random error on a probability scale compressed at 0 and 1 pulls the *mean* toward 0.5. They argue this does not affect the median.
  2. Information diversity among forecasters.

  They propose the median to tell the two apart. This is the key overlap: the idea that noise justifies extremizing already exists. A Bayesian sampler regresses each person's *expected* judgment toward 0.5, which would also shift the median and break that diagnostic. That difference is a clean new prediction.
- **Satopää et al. 2021 BIN model**, https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2020.3882. Decomposes Good Judgment Project (GJP) accuracy into bias, information and noise. Noise reduction dominates. It is a statistical model, not a sampler.
- **Lee & Danileiko 2014**, https://doi.org/10.1017/s1930297500005799, and **Turner et al. 2014**, https://doi.org/10.1007/s10994-013-5401-4. Cognitive-model and recalibration aggregation using linear-in-log-odds (LLO) calibration.
- **Zhu et al. 2022**, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2022.105022. Sampler model linking coherence and accuracy, with poker experts. It is the only application to expert forecasters, and not to tournaments.

**Still open:** fitting the sampler (N, β) to GJP data, the mean–variance signature across forecasters, and deriving the optimal extremizing parameter from the fitted N and β.

## D. Many Labs heterogeneity from scale, baseline or reliability
**Closest papers:**
- **Olsson-Collentine 2020**, https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000294. Names the reliability mechanism itself but reports no evidence for it in their data.
- **Olsson-Collentine et al. 2023**, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/jnb6e. Simulation: measurement error usually makes estimated heterogeneity too low, by 15–60%. It inflates heterogeneity only in narrow cases, such as zero true heterogeneity with a large effect.
- **Beinhauer, Fünderich & Renkewitz 2025**, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/u6anb_v1. In 12 multisite projects, correcting for reliability did not reduce heterogeneity.
- **Fünderich et al. 2025, "Under my umbrella"**, https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-025-02879-w. Rating-scale bounds make a homogeneous raw effect heterogeneous in Cohen's d. Illustrated with Many Labs data.
- **Fünderich et al. 2025, non-linearity preprint**, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/s82zr_v3. Site baselines combined with a concave or ceiling response function produce heterogeneity. Diagnosed within each of 55 multi-lab datasets. Explicitly motivated by the Olsson-Collentine correlation.
- **Frank & Heene 2024**, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/txnpg. Ordinal instead of linear models barely change heterogeneity estimates.

**Still open:**
- One calibrated simulation that reproduces the tau–effect-size correlation *across* effects. All existing work is within one effect.
- A binary-outcome arm (risk difference vs log-odds) for psychology.

**Constraints:**
- Olsson-Collentine analysed binary outcomes as log-odds ratios, which stay homogeneous under a logit latent model. The binary arm therefore needs a stated latent-threshold mechanism.
- The reliability arm is already weakened by the 2023 and 2025 papers.

**Scoop risk:** the LMU META-REP project on "just methodological artefacts?" (Heene, Renkewitz and colleagues) is working on this question.

## E. Small-sample model predicting feedback shifts and the description–experience gap
**Closest papers:**
- **BEAST, Erev et al. 2017**, https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000062. Parameters fitted on the CPC15 choice-prediction competition data, then used to predict choice rates per problem and per block in advance. Block 1 has no feedback; blocks 2–5 have feedback.
- **Plonsky et al. 2025**, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-025-02267-6. BEAST with frozen parameters predicts the CPC18 competition data and the choices13k dataset. BEAST-GB adds machine learning on top.
- **Erev et al. 2010 competition**, https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.683. Small-sample models won the experience condition. Description was predicted by a separate model.
- **Plonsky, Teodorescu & Erev 2015**, https://doi.org/10.1037/a0039413.
- **Wulff et al. 2018**, https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000115. Moderator analyses only. No generative sampling model fitted to the database.

**Still open:**
- Whether a minimal 1–2 parameter k-sample model recovers the feedback shift itself, used directly as the target.
- A fixed-parameter prediction of the description–experience gap per problem across the Wulff database. No one has done this.

**Constraints:**
- CPC feedback blocks also show forgone outcomes, so the hot-stove mechanism cannot operate there. Only small-sample reliance can be tested.
- https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-67729-x (2026, seven experiments) finds feedback raises risk-taking *before* any outcome is experienced. That argues against a learning account of the block-1 shift. Read it before committing to E.

## F. Hard–easy effect across the Confidence Database
**Closest papers:**
- **Guggenmos 2022**, https://doi.org/10.7554/elife.75420. A bias-free noisy observer shows a hard–easy "statistical artefact". Validated on one dataset only.
- **Merkle 2009**, https://doi.org/10.3758/pbr.16.1.204. Derives when random error produces the effect.
- **Suantak et al. 1996**, https://doi.org/10.1006/obhd.1996.0074. Fits a model of the effect in probability calibration.
- **Khalvati et al. 2021**, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-25419-4. Bayesian model, tested on monkey data.
- **Confidence Database work on other questions:**
  - Rahnev et al. 2020, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-019-0813-1: the database paper; its analyses are not about calibration.
  - Hellmann et al. 2023, https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0001524: compares 14 confidence models; not about calibration.
  - Boundy-Singer et al. 2023, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-022-01464-x: confidence model fits; not about calibration.
  - Jin et al. 2022, https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-022-02063-7: across-subject confidence–accuracy correlation.

**Still open:** fit noise for each dataset and predict that dataset's hard–easy magnitude, then compare with observation.

**Constraint:** many datasets use 1–4 rating scales with a single difficulty level. The usable subset (probability-scale confidence plus varied difficulty) may be small, so check it first.

## G. Advice taking as Bayesian cue integration with trimodal weights
**Closest papers:**
- **Ravazzolo & Røisland 2011**, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.econlet.2011.03.032. Analytic Bayesian model with asymmetric knowledge of own vs advisor competence. Advice weight falls smoothly with distance. No weight-of-advice (WOA) distributions.
- **Himmelstein 2022**, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmp.2022.102695. "Dual hurdle" model: a discrete decline / adopt / compromise stage followed by continuous averaging. Fits the spikes at 0 and 1, but the modes are built in as parameters rather than generated.
- **Rebholz et al. 2023**, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/y8x92. Classifies Bayesian vs choosing vs compromising strategies.
- **Moussaïd et al. 2013**, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0078433. Empirical keep / compromise / adopt map as a function of distance.
- **Schultze et al. 2015**, https://doi.org/10.1017/s1930297500003922. Curvilinear WOA–distance relation, not modelled.
- **Hütter & Ache 2016**, https://doi.org/10.1017/s193029750000382x. Information-asymmetry account stated in words and tested by experiment.

**Still open:** a generative model in which the own-reasons asymmetry itself produces the trimodal distribution and the curvilinear WOA–distance curve, fitted quantitatively.

**Design flag:** pure precision-weighted averaging gives a smooth WOA distribution. Spikes need a discrete choice or threshold stage. Himmelstein's model is the benchmark to beat.

## H. Inner crowd as an autocorrelated sampler
**Closest papers:**
- **Dasgupta, Schulz & Gershman 2017**, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2017.05.001. Simulates the crowd within as a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampler, showing that averaging two guesses from one chain gains less than averaging across chains. Qualitative only: no delay dimension and no fit.
- **Rauhut & Lorenz 2011**, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmp.2010.10.002. Expresses a second guess as a number of "other people": 1.11 when immediate and 1.32 after 3 weeks. Their data reject independent draws from an internal distribution. Not a process model.
- **Zhu et al. 2024 Autocorrelated Bayesian Sampler**, https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000427. Full text checked: it does not treat the inner crowd.
- **Zhu et al. 2022**, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1010312. A sampler fitted to the autocorrelation of repeated estimates, not to the accuracy of averaged pairs.
- **Delay data to fit:**
  - Vul & Pashler 2008, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2008.02136.x
  - Steegen et al. 2014, https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00786 (public raw data)
  - van Dolder & van den Assem 2018, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-017-0247-6

**Still open:** the whole test. Map delay onto chain decorrelation and fit it to these three delay datasets, checking against the Rauhut & Lorenz non-independence finding. Residual risk is a CogSci proceedings paper that OpenAlex indexes poorly.
